claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite with discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
A thin, conformal Ni coating is applied to W surfaces before composite consolidation.
The Ni coating forms a continuous Ni-based interfacial layer between W and Cu.
The Ni-based interfacial layer produces a stable, bonded W/Ni/Cu interface.
The Ni-based interfacial layer acts as a diffusion barrier.
The Ni interlayer reduces interfacial energy between the W and Cu phases.
The Ni interlayer improves wetting between W and Cu during high-temperature treatment.
The Ni interlayer limits atomic interdiffusion during processing and irradiation.
Limiting interdiffusion suppresses the kinetics of phase separation and interfacial void nucleation.
Ni pre-coating suppresses phase separation and mitigates interfacial void formation during processing and service.
Enhanced interfacial bonding and reduced void formation improve the composite's thermal conductivity.
Ni-coated W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated W–Cu under high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Cu typically develops phase separation and interfacial voids during heat treatment and irradiation.
Phase separation and interfacial voids lower the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu.
The beneficial effect is expected to persist at processing temperatures and irradiation fluxes typical of plasma-facing-material/cooling-component interfaces.
Excessive processing temperatures or prolonged irradiation may destabilize the Ni layer and reduce its effectiveness.
The magnitude of the conductivity improvement depends on Ni-coating uniformity, coating thickness, and processing parameters.
